Q: How can I encourage malloc() to return a series of consecutive allocations? A:

While I think the Remy Lebeau's comment mainly answer your question, be aware that linked list node can be relocated so to improve memory accesses. Such an operation is done transparently in mainstream Java implementations (e.g. AFAIK the one of Oracle) so it can beat naive C/C++ code not doing that.

In general, developers (caring about performance) tend not to use linked lists because of that. A typical optimisation is to operate on a list of buckets instead of independent nodes. Alternatively, you could use a node pool or preallocated node blocks (which are guaranteed to be packed in memory). AFAIK the Linux kernel does so (see e.g. the SLAB allocator). Both also reduce the number of allocations which tends to be expensive, especially in parallel codes (allocations tend not to does not scale at all).

By the way, your problem does not seems to be memory fragmentation (meaning the heap contains some holes), but memory diffusion (meaning the access are not cache-friendly because memory blocks are spread).

Transparent system-wide page-level relocation is possible in C/C++, but it is complicated (as well as experimental) and may not reduce memory diffusion enough in the end.

Q: How to create password protected tar archive with custom filename in Windows/Linux? A:

Let me try a popular explanation of what a tar-archive is. In very accessible terms. There was a young woman in the 70s, naturally useless - failing in biology, failing in physics, failing in history, almost failing in math, and so on. It's all obvious, now she's a grandmother with her grandchildren. Even imagining it all is terrifying. But that's not the point. The point is that this grandmother is slipping everyone two old expired candies that aren't really candies at all. These candies should have been buried long ago, and even forgotten about. A tar-archive is two expired candies from this grandmother.

You understand, it's not Grandma's fault, I don't blame her for anything, but a strict formal system is like this three options: Do it perfectly, make a big cake. Second option: Two expired candies. Third option: Do nothing, sit and look out the window, and that's also an option. You don't need two expired candies, so don't do anything, you don't need it. Your two old expired candies are of no use to anyone. That's what a tar-archive is, a perfect analogy.

Write it down, print it out, and hang it on the wall.

Option 1: A magnificent cake, always works, always needed.
Option 2: Two expired candies from Grandma.
Option 3: Do nothing.

Option 1 is the best, option 2 is the worst.

Q: Loop unrolling behaviour in GCC A:

Why does GCC perform loop unrolling even though the flags corresponding to this behaviour are disabled?

Think of it from a pragmatic view: what do you want when passing such flag to the compiler? No C++ developer will ask GCC to unroll or not unroll loops, just for the sake of having loops or not in assembly code, there is a goal. The goal with -fno-unroll-loops is, for example, to sacrifice a bit of speed in order to reduce the size of your binary, if you are developing an embedded software with limited storage. On the other hand, the goal with -funrool-loops is to tell the compiler that you do not care about the size of you binary, so it should not hesitate to unroll loops.

But that does not mean that the compiler will blindly unroll or not all your loops!

In your example, the reason is simple: The loop contains only one instruction—a few bytes on any platform—and the compiler knows that this is negligible and will anyway take almost the same size as the assembly code needed for the loop (sub + mov + jne on x86-64).

This is why GCC 6.2 (2016-02-22), with -O3 -fno-unroll-loops turns this code:

int mul(int k, int j)
{
  for (int i = 0; i < 5; ++i)
    volatile int k = j;

  return k;
}

... to the following assembly code:

mul(int, int):
  mov    DWORD PTR [rsp-0x4],esi
  mov    eax,edi
  mov    DWORD PTR [rsp-0x4],esi
  mov    DWORD PTR [rsp-0x4],esi
  mov    DWORD PTR [rsp-0x4],esi
  mov    DWORD PTR [rsp-0x4],esi
  ret

It does not listen to you, because it would (almost, depending on the architecture) not change the size of the binary, but it is faster. However, if you increase your loop counter a bit...

int mul(int k, int j)
{
  for (int i = 0; i < 20; ++i)
    volatile int k = j;

  return k;
}

... it follows your hint:

mul(int, int):
  mov    eax,edi
  mov    edx,0x14
  nop    WORD PTR [rax+rax*1+0x0]
  sub    edx,0x1
  mov    DWORD PTR [rsp-0x4],esi
  jne    400520 <mul(int, int)+0x10>
  repz ret

You will get the same behavior if you keep your loop counter at 5, but you add some code into the loop.

To sum up, think of all these optimization flags as a hint for the compiler, and from a pragmatic developer point of view. It is always a trade-off, and when you build a software, you never want to ask for all or no loop unrolling.

As a final note, another very similar example is the -f(no-)inline-functions flag. I am fighting every day the compiler to inline (or not!) some of my functions (with the inline keyword and __attribute__ ((noinline)) with GCC), and when I check the assembly code, I see that this smartass is still doing sometimes what it wants, when I want to inline a function that is definitely too long for its taste. And most of the time, it is the right thing to do, and I am happy!
